lessons.title: Measuring Social Development
lessons.description: Why gender and health are sharper measures of progress than national wealth alone.
lessons.content_html:
Beyond GDP — Measuring How Lives Are Lived

A country’s wealth is one story. A country’s daily life is another. Geographers studying social development ask a different question from those measuring economic development: not ‘how rich is this country?’ but ‘how well are people in this country actually living?’ The answers can surprise you. Two countries with similar GDPs can have very different rates of literacy, life expectancy and women’s rights.

Key Fact

Economic development measures wealth (GDP, GNI). Social development measures how people actually live — their health, education and equality. Two countries can have similar GDP but very different daily lives.

Health as a Measure

Health indicators reveal the strength of public services, food supply and clean water. Life expectancy is one of the sharpest signals: babies born in Japan today can expect to live to around 84, while those born in Sierra Leone may only reach the early 60s. Infant mortality rate is even more sensitive — a high rate often signals weak maternal care, poor sanitation or malnutrition. South Asia has cut its infant mortality in half since 2000, but rates in parts of sub-Saharan Africa remain among the world’s highest.

Other health measures fill in the picture. The number of doctors per 1,000 people, access to vaccines, and rates of HIV, malaria and tuberculosis all sharpen the comparison. The lower-income world made huge gains on these indicators between 2000 and 2020 — child deaths halved — before the COVID-19 pandemic temporarily reversed some progress.

Equatorial Guinea has a high GDP per person, thanks to oil. Yet 50% of its people lack access to safe water, life expectancy sits below 60 and most live in poverty — the wealth flows to a small elite. Costa Rica has a much lower GDP per person but boasts higher literacy, longer life expectancy and stronger gender equality. GDP measures the size of an economy. It does not measure how the money is shared.

Gender as a Measure

Gender equality is now central to social development. Geographers and the United Nations look at the share of girls completing primary and secondary school, the share of women in paid work and parliament, and gendered measures of health like maternal mortality. The United Nations Gender Inequality Index (GII) rolls these together into a single score: the lower the score, the closer the country is to equality.

The story varies sharply by region. In Rwanda, more than 60% of MPs are women — the highest share in the world. In parts of sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, by contrast, fewer than half of girls complete secondary school, and women still earn less than men for the same work in almost every country. Gender data shows progress as well as gaps: girls’ school enrolment in South Asia has risen sharply since 2000.

Key Fact

Gender equality is measured through girls’ school enrolment, women in paid work and parliament, and maternal mortality. Together these capture how power, money and survival are shared between the sexes.

The Development Continuum

The old labels ‘developed’ and ‘developing’ suggest two clear groups, but geographers now picture a development continuum — a sliding scale on which every country sits somewhere different. Sweden and Sierra Leone are at opposite ends; India, Indonesia and South Africa sit in the middle and are moving fast. The continuum captures change. Vietnam, once near the bottom of the social development scale, has cut child mortality, raised life expectancy and improved girls’ education within a generation.

A Closing — or Widening — Gap?

For most of the 21st century, the social development gap has narrowed. Life expectancy has risen worldwide. Child deaths have fallen. Girls’ school enrolment has climbed. The Millennium and Sustainable Development Goals helped focus international funding on these targets. But progress is uneven. Sub-Saharan Africa still lags on almost every health indicator. Conflict in places like South Sudan and Yemen reverses gains overnight. Climate change threatens to widen rather than close future gaps.

A growing economy does not automatically translate into longer, fairer lives. Some oil-rich states have a high GDP but high gender inequality; some lower-GDP states like Sri Lanka and Cuba have life expectancy approaching that of HICs. The Human Development Index (HDI) combines income, education and life expectancy precisely because no single number tells the full story. Geographers use a basket of indicators — health, education, gender, poverty — to build a fuller picture of how a country is really doing.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 4-mark ‘Compare’ questions on development indicators, name your two indicators and your two countries up front: ‘Compare life expectancy in Japan (84 years) with Sierra Leone (around 60).’ For 6-mark ‘Explain with Example’ questions, link a social indicator to a real outcome, e.g. ‘Higher girls’ school enrolment in Bangladesh has lowered child marriage and infant mortality.’ Generic answers about ‘some countries’ lose marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Social development measures how people actually live — their health, education and gender equality — rather than just national wealth.
  • Health indicators (life expectancy, infant mortality) and gender indicators (girls’ schooling, women in parliament, maternal mortality) reveal gaps that GDP hides.
  • Countries sit on a development continuum that shifts over time; the global gap has narrowed since 2000 but climate change and conflict threaten progress.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best defines life expectancy?
A) The total population of a country in a given year
B) The average number of years a newborn baby is expected to live
C) The number of births per 1,000 women each year
D) The percentage of girls enrolled in primary school
practice_questions.marks: B) The average number of years a newborn baby is expected to live [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe one indicator of gender equality.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a clear indicator with brief development, e.g. the share of women in parliament shows whether women hold decision-making power; Rwanda has the highest share at over 60%. Secure: indicator named with limited development. Developing: vague reference to women's rights. Emerging: no specific indicator.

practice_questions.text: Explain why gender and health are useful measures of social development.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: clear chain — gender equality and health show whether national wealth is reaching ordinary lives; high GDP can hide poor health or unequal opportunities; rising life expectancy and girls’ school enrolment signal real improvements in everyday life. Secure: one mechanism with effect. Developing: states they are useful without explaining. Emerging: no link to social development.

practice_questions.text: Compare GDP and infant mortality rate as measures of development.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explicit comparison using linking words on at least two points — both are widely used and easy to compare across countries, however GDP measures national wealth whereas infant mortality measures the chance of dying before age one; GDP can be high in unequal oil states whereas infant mortality reveals weak maternal care, sanitation and nutrition. Secure: one explicit comparison. Developing: lists features of each separately. Emerging: only one feature named.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a country can have a high GDP but low social development. Use a named example.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: developed account using a named country (e.g. Equatorial Guinea, Saudi Arabia, oil-rich Gulf states) showing that GDP is high because of oil or another resource, but wealth concentrates in an elite, women’s rights are limited, life expectancy may be low, and access to clean water and schooling is poor. Secure: named example with two indicators but limited locational detail. Developing: generic with one indicator. Emerging: vague reference without named place.

practice_questions.text:
“A single development measure can never tell the full story of how developed a country is.”
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument with named examples weighing the strengths of single measures (GDP per capita is comparable, easy to calculate, useful for policymakers) against weaknesses (hides inequality, ignores gender, ignores environment, e.g. Equatorial Guinea high GDP but low life expectancy) and the value of composite measures like HDI or a basket of indicators reaching a justified judgement (e.g. a single number is useful as a quick comparison but a basket gives the truer picture). Secure: balanced argument with one named example. Developing: one-sided or generic. Emerging: simple agreement or disagreement without evidence.

lessons.title: Social Challenges in Africa & South Asia
lessons.description: Education, child labour, refugees and infant mortality across sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia.
lessons.content_html:
Two Regions, Big Social Challenges

Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia together hold over a third of the world’s population and most of its extreme poverty. Both regions have made real progress this century — child mortality has fallen, more children are in school, life expectancy is up — but four challenges still loom large: getting girls through school, ending child labour, supporting refugees, and reducing infant mortality.

Key Fact

The four main social challenges in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia are getting girls through school, ending child labour, supporting refugees, and reducing infant mortality. All four are linked — tackling one helps the others.

Education and Girls

Universal primary school is one of the most reliable ways to break the cycle of poverty. Girls who finish primary and secondary school marry later, have fewer children, earn more and lose fewer babies before age one. South Asia has made huge progress — girls’ primary enrolment is now near boys’ in India, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka. Sub-Saharan Africa lags: in countries like Niger and Chad, only around half of girls complete primary school, and far fewer reach secondary.

Reasons why girls drop out are stubborn: school fees, the cost of uniforms and books, long unsafe walks to class, lack of girls’ toilets, early marriage, and the assumption that boys’ education is more valuable. The BRAC schools network in Bangladesh built one-room village schools targeted at girls and now educates more than a million children. International targets, especially the UN Sustainable Development Goal 4, push every country to deliver inclusive education.

Each extra year a girl spends in secondary school raises her future income by around 15%. Better-educated mothers are more likely to vaccinate children, less likely to die in childbirth and less likely to lose a baby in its first year. Education is, in development terms, a multiplier — gains in one generation feed into the next.

Child Labour

Roughly 160 million children worldwide work in jobs that should be done by adults — in farms, mines, factories, brick kilns and homes as domestic servants. Many are in South Asia, particularly India and Pakistan, and in sub-Saharan Africa, especially in cocoa farms in Ivory Coast and Ghana. Children work because families need their income; a missed school year often means missed school forever. Hazardous work damages bodies still growing — spinal injuries from hauling bricks, lung disease from textile dust, eye damage from carpet weaving.

Tackling child labour is hard because it is woven into household survival. Successful approaches combine free school meals (so children eat when they study), conditional cash transfers (governments pay families to keep children in class), and adult literacy programmes (so parents earn more and rely less on children’s wages). Brazil’s Bolsa Família is a model now copied in several African and South Asian countries.

Refugees and International Migration

Conflict, persecution and climate change push millions to leave home. Sub-Saharan Africa hosts more than 7 million refugees and asylum seekers, with major flows from South Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Somalia. Most cross into neighbouring countries — Uganda hosts more than 1.5 million people from neighbouring states. South Asia’s refugee picture is dominated by the Rohingya: nearly a million fled Myanmar to Bangladesh after 2017, where most still live in the world’s largest refugee settlement at Cox’s Bazar.

Refugees face overcrowded camps, limited schooling and irregular work. International responses include the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR), national resettlement programmes, and bilateral agreements between donor and host countries. The challenge is that refugees usually need years of support, not weeks — emergency aid alone cannot rebuild a life.

Key Fact

Refugees flee war, persecution and disaster — for example, the Rohingya from Myanmar to Bangladesh after 2017, and South Sudanese into Uganda. Most stay in neighbouring LICs, not in HICs, often for years.

Infant Mortality and Health

In sub-Saharan Africa, around 27 babies in every 1,000 die before their first birthday — ten times the rate in HICs. Causes are linked: malnutrition, unclean water, poor maternal health, weak vaccination coverage, malaria and HIV. South Asia’s rates have fallen sharply (especially in Bangladesh and Sri Lanka) but Pakistan and Afghanistan still struggle.

Solutions follow the diagnosis: rolling out vaccines (the GAVI alliance now reaches more than half of the world’s children), training community midwives, distributing insecticide-treated bed nets, and providing oral rehydration salts for diarrhoea, the second-biggest killer of under-fives. UN Sustainable Development Goal 3 targets a global infant mortality rate of 12 per 1,000 by 2030.

Top-down projects are large-scale, often funded by the World Bank or UN, like national vaccination drives or new rural roads. They reach millions but can miss local needs. Bottom-up projects, run by NGOs and community groups, are smaller and slower — like BRAC’s village schools or local health worker training — but fit the daily realities of the people they serve. The most successful countries combine both.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 6-mark questions on social challenges, name the country and the project: ‘BRAC schools in Bangladesh educate over a million children, mostly girls’ beats ‘a charity project in Asia’. For 8-mark evaluations, weigh top-down approaches against bottom-up ones, and reach a clear judgement: ‘On balance, vaccination programmes work top-down but girls’ education works best bottom-up.’
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia face four key social challenges: girls’ education, child labour, refugees and infant mortality — all linked through poverty and weak services.
  • South Asia has made faster progress on schooling and infant mortality (e.g. Bangladesh, Sri Lanka) than parts of sub-Saharan Africa where rates remain high (e.g. Niger, Chad).
  • Successful responses combine top-down programmes (UN goals, GAVI vaccines) with bottom-up projects (BRAC schools, community midwives, conditional cash transfers).

B) A person forced to leave their country to escape war, persecution or disaster

practice_questions.text: Describe one cause of high infant mortality in sub-Saharan Africa.

practice_questions.text: Explain why girls in many parts of sub-Saharan Africa do not complete secondary school.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: clear chain — school fees and uniform costs are out of reach for poorer families; long, unsafe walks to school deter parents; some girls leave for early marriage; lack of girls’ toilets pushes older girls out. Secure: one cause with brief explanation. Developing: states girls drop out without explanation. Emerging: no causal link.

practice_questions.text: Compare top-down and bottom-up approaches to tackling social challenges.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explicit comparison using linking words on at least two points — both aim to improve quality of life, but top-down is large-scale and funded by governments or UN whereas bottom-up is small-scale and run with local communities; top-down can deliver mass vaccination quickly whereas bottom-up fits local culture and needs more closely. “Education is the single most effective way to tackle social challenges in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia.”

lessons.title: Consumerism & the Environment
lessons.description: How rising consumer demand drives ecological footprints, food miles and the global e-waste problem.
lessons.content_html:
A Consuming Planet

Every purchase has a hidden geography. The clothes in your wardrobe, the phone in your pocket and the strawberries on your breakfast all rely on land, water and energy somewhere in the world. As global incomes rise, demand for those goods rises too — and so does the strain on the environment. Geographers measure that strain through the ecological footprint: the total area of productive land and water needed to support a person’s lifestyle.

Key Fact

An ecological footprint measures the productive land and water needed to support a lifestyle. The average UK footprint is about 4.4 global hectares per person; if everyone lived like the UK, we would need around three planets.

Why Footprints Are Growing

The richer a country, the bigger its footprint. The average person in the United States needs around 8 global hectares; in India, the figure is closer to 1.2. Rising NIC incomes — especially in China and India — are pushing global demand for cars, meat, electronics and air travel up sharply. Online shopping, cheap flights and 24-hour delivery raise consumption per person even within HICs. Globalisation lets a UK shopper buy strawberries grown in Spain in February, but the energy cost of the cold-chain transport still falls somewhere.

Food Miles and Hidden Costs

Food miles are one part of the picture. Out-of-season strawberries flown from Egypt or Kenya, beef shipped from Brazil, lamb chilled from New Zealand — all rack up emissions in flights, lorries and refrigeration. A UK supermarket basket can have ingredients from 30 countries. Long supply chains also leave consumers far from the conditions in which their food is grown, masking unfair pay or environmental damage.

Food miles are not the whole story. A tomato grown in a UK heated greenhouse in January can carry a higher footprint than one shipped chilled from southern Spain. Greenhouse gases per kilogramme depend on energy used to grow as well as transport. Geographers therefore look at the full carbon footprint of a food, not just the distance.

Palm oil hides in around half of supermarket products — biscuits, soap, lipstick, biofuel. Demand has driven huge clearance of tropical rainforest in Indonesia and Malaysia, threatening orangutans and releasing locked-up carbon as peatland burns. Sustainable certification schemes try to track ethical sources, but auditing thousands of plantations is hard. Buying habits in HICs end up reshaping ecosystems on the other side of the world.

E-Waste and the Throwaway Economy

Electronic devices have a short life. Phones get replaced every 2–3 years, laptops every 4–5. The world now generates more than 60 million tonnes of e-waste a year — the equivalent of 350 cruise ships of broken phones, laptops and televisions. Most contains valuable metals (copper, gold, lithium) but also toxic materials like lead, mercury and cadmium.

Much HIC e-waste used to be shipped to Ghana, Nigeria or India, often illegally. At the Agbogbloshie dumpsite in Accra, Ghana, families burned old wires and computer parts to extract copper, breathing in toxic fumes. Children worked in the smoke. Stricter international rules under the Basel Convention have reduced these flows, but poor recycling infrastructure means much e-waste still ends up where it should not.

Key Fact

Consumer choices in HICs reshape environments in LICs — through palm-oil deforestation, food-mile emissions and shipped e-waste. The connection is invisible at the till but visible on the ground.

Climate Change as the Master Multiplier

Rising consumption is a major driver of climate change — through energy use, transport, deforestation and intensive farming. Climate change in turn worsens almost every challenge we have already met: more drought across the Sahel, more intense cyclones in Bangladesh, melting glaciers reducing summer river flow in northern India, and rising seas threatening Pacific small-island states like Tuvalu and Kiribati. Vulnerable communities tend to be those who consumed least.

Individual responses include: choosing seasonal local food, eating less meat (a kilo of beef takes 25 times the water of a kilo of grain), repairing rather than replacing electronics, and reducing fast-fashion buys. Government responses include carbon taxes, plastic bag charges, mandatory recycling, and right-to-repair laws (the EU and UK now require some electronics to be repairable). International responses include the Paris Agreement and the UN’s wider climate finance commitments to help LICs adapt. None alone is enough; together they begin to shift the curve.

Connecting the Threads

Consumerism, food miles and e-waste are not three separate problems. They are three sides of the same global economy, in which choices made in HIC supermarkets and online stores ripple outwards into rainforests, dumpsites and atmospheric carbon. The questions for geographers are not just ‘what is happening?’ but ‘who pays the costs?’ and ‘how could we do this differently?’
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 6-mark ‘Explain with Example’ questions, anchor every consumer-environment link in a real product and a real place — ‘palm oil for biscuits has driven peatland fires in Indonesia’ beats ‘food affects ecosystems’. For 8-mark evaluations, weigh individual versus government action and reach a clear judgement; markers want to see ‘On balance, individual choices help but only carbon taxes and right-to-repair laws shift behaviour at scale.’
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • An ecological footprint measures the land and water needed to support a lifestyle; HIC footprints are several times bigger than those of LIC residents.
  • Food miles, palm-oil deforestation and shipped e-waste (e.g. Agbogbloshie in Ghana) link consumer choices to environmental damage on the other side of the world.
  • Climate change ties the picture together — consumption drives emissions, and the most vulnerable communities, in places like Bangladesh, Tuvalu and the Sahel, tend to be those who consumed least.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best defines food miles?
A) The total carbon released in growing a food product
B) The distance food travels from where it is produced to where it is consumed
C) The shelf life of a food once packaged

practice_questions.text: Describe one impact of e-waste on the environment.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a clear impact with brief development, e.g. burning electronics to extract copper releases toxic chemicals like lead and mercury into soil and air, harming local communities. practice_questions.text: Explain why ecological footprints are larger in HICs than in LICs.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: clear chain — HIC residents earn more so eat more meat, fly more, drive more and buy more electronics; each activity uses more land, water and energy; cheaper imports raise consumption further. Secure: one mechanism with effect. Developing: states richer countries use more resources without explaining. Emerging: no causal link.

practice_questions.text: Compare food miles and full carbon footprint as measures of food's environmental impact.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explicit comparison using linking words on at least two points — both try to capture environmental impact, however food miles count only the distance whereas full carbon footprint includes growing, refrigeration and energy; food miles can mislead (a heated UK greenhouse tomato may have a bigger footprint than one shipped chilled from Spain) whereas full carbon footprint gives a fairer picture. Secure: one explicit comparison. Developing: lists features separately. Emerging: only one feature named.

practice_questions.text: Explain how consumerism in HICs has changed environments in LICs and NICs. Use named examples.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: developed account with named products and places (e.g. palm oil clearance in Indonesia/Malaysia for biscuits and soap, Agbogbloshie e-waste site in Ghana, Brazilian beef driving Amazon clearance, food miles for Kenyan cut flowers and out-of-season strawberries) covering at least two impacts — deforestation, soil degradation, carbon emissions, toxic pollution. Secure: named example with two impacts but limited detail. Developing: generic with one impact. Emerging: vague reference without named place.

practice_questions.text:
“Reducing consumerism is the most important way to protect the global environment.”
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument with named examples weighing strengths of cutting consumption (lower food miles, less palm oil clearance in Indonesia, less e-waste at Agbogbloshie, lower greenhouse gas emissions) against alternatives (technology-driven solutions like renewable energy, government-led policy like carbon taxes and right-to-repair laws, international agreements like the Paris Agreement) and reaching a justified judgement (e.g. cutting consumption is essential but only laws and global agreements deliver change at scale). Secure: balanced argument with one named example. Developing: one-sided or generic. Emerging: simple agreement or disagreement without evidence.

lessons.title: Restoring & Managing Habitats
lessons.description: Wetland restoration, ecotourism and managing habitats for a sustainable future.
lessons.content_html:
Why Restore Habitats?

Across the UK and tropical world, human activity has drained, polluted or fragmented natural habitats. Once a habitat is damaged, the species and services it provides — clean water, flood protection, carbon storage, food — begin to disappear. Habitat restoration is the deliberate effort to reverse that damage and rebuild a functioning ecosystem.

Restoration is not the same as conservation. Conservation protects what is already there; restoration rebuilds what has been lost. Both are needed because the UK is one of the most nature-depleted countries in Europe, and tropical biomes are under intense pressure from logging, fishing and tourism.

Key Fact

Restored habitats provide ecosystem services — clean water, flood storage, carbon capture and biodiversity. The UN estimates every £1 spent on restoration returns up to £30 in benefits over time.

Wetland Restoration in the UK

A wetland is land that is wet for much of the year. The UK has lost roughly 90% of its wetlands since 1700, mostly to drainage for farmland and building. Wetland restoration reverses this by blocking drains, breaching old flood banks and letting rivers spill onto their floodplains again.

The Great Fen project, started in 2001, aims to link Woodwalton Fen and Holme Fen by restoring 3,700 hectares of farmland between them. Drainage ditches are blocked, peat is rewetted and species-poor fields become reedbed, wet grassland and open water. Cranes returned to breed in the area in 2007 after a 400-year absence, and water voles, otters and bitterns are now established.

The project also stores carbon — rewetted peat stops releasing CO2 from oxidation — and reduces flood risk downstream by holding back water during heavy rain. Local farmers are paid through agri-environment schemes to manage the wetter land.

Wetland restoration delivers several services at once. The wetter peat locks in carbon, the new reedbeds filter pollutants from upstream farms, and the deeper, slower water provides flood storage that protects towns downstream. For local communities, restored fens become birdwatching destinations that bring visitors and small business income.

Key Fact

The Great Fen project has rewetted thousands of hectares of drained Cambridgeshire farmland, returning rare species (cranes, bitterns) while storing carbon and reducing downstream flood risk.

Tourism, Coral Reefs and Two Contrasting Environments

Tourism is one of the world’s biggest industries. It can pour money into local economies, but it can also wreck the very habitats people travel to see. The pressure shows clearly in two contrasting environments: tropical coastlines and coral reefs, and mountain or rainforest interiors.

On reefs around the Maldives, Belize and Indonesia, careless snorkelling, anchor damage, reef-walking and sunscreen pollution bleach corals and break their fragile structures. Hotels built on mangrove coastlines remove the natural buffer that protected those same beaches from storms. The very thing tourists visit can be destroyed within a few decades.

Sustainable Tourism: Three Linked Ideas

Ecotourism means small-scale visits to sensitive environments where most of the money stays with local people and the activity itself helps protect the habitat. Costa Rica is the global model: roughly a quarter of its land is protected, and visitors pay national park fees that fund rangers, replanting and species monitoring.

Ethical tourism goes further. It asks whether local workers are paid fairly, whether sacred sites are respected, and whether profits leak back to overseas tour operators. Responsible travel is the personal version of the same idea: choosing low-carbon transport, refilling water bottles, and avoiding wildlife attractions that exploit animals.

In Sabah, Malaysian Borneo, ecotourism lodges along the Kinabatangan River employ local guides as boatmen and trackers. Visitors pay to see orangutans and pygmy elephants in protected forest corridors. The income gives villagers a reason to keep the forest standing rather than sell it for palm oil. Lodges use solar power, treat their wastewater on-site and cap visitor numbers per boat trip to limit disturbance.

Managing Reefs and Coastlines

For coral reefs, sustainable management combines several tools. Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) ban fishing and anchoring in the most sensitive zones. Mooring buoys stop boats dropping anchors onto living coral. Visitor caps limit how many snorkellers can enter a reef section per day. Education briefings remind tourists not to touch coral or feed fish.

Tourist taxes can fund the management itself. The Maldives charges a Green Tax of US$6 per night, ring-fenced for environmental projects. Belize uses cruise-ship passenger fees to pay for reef monitoring inside its barrier-reef system, the second largest in the world.

Sustainable Futures for Habitats

Restoration and ecotourism work best together. Tourism revenue funds the rangers and scientists who replant mangroves or grow corals on artificial reefs; restored habitats then attract more visitors. The challenge is keeping numbers low enough that the cure does not become the next disease.

Looking ahead, governments are setting bigger targets. The UK is committed to protecting 30% of land and sea by 2030, and global agreements signed in 2022 set the same goal worldwide. Hitting these targets will need wetland rewetting, marine reserves, ecotourism revenue and tougher rules on sunscreen, plastic and cruise-ship discharge all working together.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For the 8-mark ‘Evaluate’ question on habitat management, mark a clear judgement at the start and end of your answer — do not just list strategies. Use a named UK example (the Great Fen) and a named tropical example (Belize’s reef tax or Borneo lodges) so your evidence is place-specific. The 6-mark ‘Explain with example’ question wants a real location, not ‘a tropical country’. Watch for the words ‘sustainable’ and ‘manage’ — they expect you to weigh environmental, economic and social impacts together.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Wetland restoration (e.g. the Great Fen) reverses past drainage, returning rare species, storing carbon and reducing flood risk downstream.
  • Tourism can damage fragile habitats, especially coral reefs and mangrove coastlines, but it can also fund their protection through ecotourism revenue and tourist taxes.
  • Ecotourism, ethical tourism and responsible travel together push the industry towards small-scale, locally owned visits that conserve habitats and biodiversity.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes ecotourism?
A) Mass tourism in coastal resorts with all-inclusive hotels
B) Small-scale tourism in fragile environments where most income stays local and supports conservation
C) Cruise tourism that visits multiple countries in one trip
D) Domestic tourism within a tourist's own country only
practice_questions.marks: B) Small-scale tourism in fragile environments where most income stays local and supports conservation [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways tourism can damage coral reefs.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per valid descriptive point, up to 2 marks. Indicative content:
• Snorkellers and reef-walkers physically break corals by touching or standing on them.
• Boat anchors dropped onto reef break the coral structure.
• Sunscreen chemicals in the water cause coral bleaching.
• Hotel construction on mangrove coastlines removes natural buffers and increases sediment runoff.
• Overfishing or fish-feeding by tour operators disturbs reef food webs.
[2 marks — accept any two distinct points clearly described]

practice_questions.text: Explain how wetland restoration can reduce flood risk for towns downstream.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark for a clear cause-effect chain. Indicative content:
• Restored wetlands store water during heavy rainfall instead of letting it run straight to the river (1).
• This slows the rate at which water reaches downstream channels, lowering peak discharge (1).
• A lower peak discharge means river levels stay below flood-defence height in towns downstream (1).
• Mastering: Sophisticated cause-effect chain with explicit reference to lag time, peak discharge or storage capacity.
• Secure: Clear three-step explanation linking storage to reduced flood risk.
• Developing: Two-step explanation; some link missing.
• Emerging: One simple point or pure description with no causal link.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare wetland restoration in the UK with ecotourism in a tropical environment as ways of managing habitats.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed comparison points needed; explicit comparative language ('whereas', 'in contrast', 'similarly') expected. Indicative content:
• Both aim to protect biodiversity, but wetland restoration in the UK rebuilds a damaged habitat, whereas ecotourism in the tropics uses visitor income to maintain a habitat that is still largely intact.
• Wetland restoration is funded by government schemes such as agri-environment payments, in contrast to ecotourism which is funded directly by tourist spending and park fees.
• Both bring economic benefits to local people; UK restoration pays farmers to manage wetter land, similarly tropical ecotourism employs local guides and lodge staff.
• A key difference is scale of visitor pressure: UK restored fens have low visitor numbers, whereas tropical reefs and rainforests must cap tourists to avoid damaging the habitat they depend on.
• Mastering: Two developed compared points with explicit linking words and named examples on both sides.
• Secure: Two clear compared points with linking words; examples present.
• Developing: Compared points present but linking words missing or one side undeveloped.
• Emerging: Two parallel descriptions with no comparison.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Using a named example, explain how ecotourism can help protect a fragile habitat.
practice_questions.marks:
Reward depth, accuracy and specificity. Indicative content (any one well-developed example is sufficient for full marks):
• Costa Rica protects roughly a quarter of its land area; national park fees pay for rangers, replanting and species monitoring, so visitor numbers directly fund conservation.
• In Sabah, Malaysian Borneo, ecotourism lodges along the Kinabatangan River employ local people as guides and trackers — villagers earn more from intact rainforest than from selling land for palm oil, so the forest is conserved.
• Lodges in Borneo cap visitor numbers per boat trip and use solar power and on-site wastewater treatment, reducing the environmental footprint of tourism on the rainforest.
• In Belize, cruise-ship passenger fees fund monitoring of the barrier reef, helping to detect bleaching and overfishing early.
• Mastering: Sustained explanation with named place, specific figures or named species, and clear cause-effect link to habitat protection.
• Secure: Named example with two clear ways tourism protects the habitat.
• Developing: Named example but vague mechanisms.
• Emerging: Generic 'African country' or 'tropical island' with no specific detail.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Restoring damaged habitats is more important than promoting ecotourism.' Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support of the statement:
• Restoration tackles damage that has already happened — once species are lost or peat dries out, ecotourism alone cannot bring them back.
• Wetland restoration provides ecosystem services beyond biodiversity (flood storage, carbon capture) that benefit everyone, not just visitors.
• Restoration projects like the Great Fen pay farmers fairly through agri-environment schemes, providing reliable, long-term funding rather than tourism revenue which can collapse during recessions or pandemics.
• Many tropical habitats are too fragile for any tourism — restoration may be the only viable option.

Arguments against the statement:
• Ecotourism funds restoration directly. Costa Rica's national park fees and Belize's cruise-ship tax pay for replanting, ranger patrols and reef monitoring.
• Without ecotourism revenue, communities in places like Borneo would have stronger economic reasons to clear forests for palm oil.
• Restoration alone cannot keep habitats intact long-term if local people see no economic benefit; ecotourism gives nature a value that competes with extractive industries.
• Many habitats (intact rainforest, healthy reefs) need maintenance not restoration — ecotourism is the right tool there.

Justified conclusion expected. Indicative judgement: both are needed and work best together — restoration repairs damage, ecotourism creates the income and political support to keep restored habitats protected.
• Mastering: Sophisticated argument with explicit judgement, named examples on both sides, and weighing of evidence.
• Secure: Clear argument with two reasoned points each side and a justified conclusion.
• Developing: Some argument both sides; conclusion present but not justified.
• Emerging: One-sided list or no clear conclusion.
[8 marks plus SPaG]

glossary_terms.definition: Working with natural processes to repair an ecosystem so its species, soils and water cycles return to a more natural state.
Land that is permanently or seasonally waterlogged, including marshes, fens, bogs and floodplain meadows.
The process of returning drained or polluted wetlands to a functioning waterlogged state by removing barriers and rewetting peat or marshland.
Tourism that involves visiting fragile natural environments in a way that protects ecosystems, supports conservation and brings income to local people.
Tourism that respects the rights, culture and economies of local people and avoids exploiting workers or communities.
Travel that takes individual responsibility for environmental, social and economic impacts and seeks to leave a destination better off.
